analysis.one_liner: Requires factories to plan and report cuts in toxic chemical waste, aiming to halve it by 1996.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 1991 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it died without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it national policy to cut toxic chemical byproducts 50 percent from 1991 levels by 1996. Any facility that files toxic release reports would have to write a detailed pollution prevention plan with numerical reduction goals, get a senior corporate officer to certify it under penalty of perjury, and file annual public progress reports. Facilities lagging behind or violating environmental rules would face mandatory audits by certified auditors, civil penalties, and possible denial of environmental permits. The bill also provided federal matching grants to states for technical assistance, especially for smaller firms, and created a demonstration program letting up to 50 well-complying facilities receive regulatory flexibility.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near or downstream from industrial facilities that handle toxic chemicals, and workers at those facilities, because the bill aimed to cut toxic releases and waste at the source rather than control them after the fact. States and small businesses would also get technical-assistance grants to help with compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Declares national policy to achieve a 50 percent reduction in toxic chemical byproduct levels by 1996 from 1991 levels.

Requires every facility that files toxic chemical release reports to prepare a pollution prevention plan with two- and five-year numerical reduction goals, and makes annual progress reports available to the public.

Requires the CEO or a senior officer to certify each plan's accuracy and implementation under penalty of perjury, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for failing to prepare or implement a plan.

Requires facilities with poor compliance histories to conduct compliance audits and implement the recommendations, and lets the EPA or states deny environmental permits to facilities that fail to prepare or implement plans.

Authorizes $10 million a year in matching grants to states for pollution prevention planning assistance, with emphasis on helping smaller facilities, workers, and community groups understand the reports.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and other facilities that use or emit toxic chemicals would bear the cost of writing plans, adopting reduction measures, conducting audits, and paying penalties for noncompliance. The federal government would fund grants, research, and the auditor certification program with appropriations of about $20 million a year.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes substantial planning, reporting, and paperwork requirements on covered facilities, and companies would bear the cost of implementing identified reduction measures unless they could show technical infeasibility or harm to product quality or health.

Plans themselves could largely be kept confidential: documents reviewed by regulators would not be deemed public records, and companies could shield competitively sensitive information, limiting what neighbors could actually learn beyond the annual reports.
Compliance costs would fall hardest on smaller firms, which is why the bill directs technical-assistance grants to them; some costs could be passed to consumers in product prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's own findings argue prevention is cost-effective for industry because cutting chemical use also cuts raw material purchases, waste handling, and liability costs, so some compliance spending would pay for itself. The main honest objection is the administrative burden and the risk that planning requirements generate documents without forcing real reductions; the bill addresses this with mandatory audits in lagging sectors, penalties, and permit denial, but also with exemptions companies could invoke. On balance it was a pollution-prevention mandate with real teeth and real escape hatches.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate simply referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee in March 1991, and the committee never took it up before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Joseph Lieberman introduced the bill on March 21, 1991, joined by original cosponsors Sen. Durenberger and Sen. Lautenberg.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
It was one of several pollution prevention bills of that era building on the Pollution Prevention Act of 1990, which had declared source reduction a national policy without mandating facility plans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that use and release toxic chemicals were better off, since they avoided the planning, audit, and reduction requirements, and no one gained the bill's promised pollution cuts.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed for mandatory facility pollution prevention plans with a 50 percent toxic byproduct reduction goal.

for.name: Sen. Dave Durenberger
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Three additional Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsorship to five, two Republicans and three Democrats.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 21, 1991 and never held a markup or reported it, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five cosponsors split two Republicans and three Democrats, but the record shows no committee or floor action against it, only inaction.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and industrial toxic chemical users
industries.note: Covered facilities would have had to write reduction plans, implement low-payback reduction measures, face audits and penalties, and risk permit denial. Their interest in the bill's fate ran against neighbors' exposure to toxic waste, though the bill's findings concede prevention can also save industry money.
The bill would have created a federal certification program for environmental auditors and required mandatory audits by certified firms, opening a new regulated market for audit services.
States could take over plan review with federal approval and receive matching grants covering up to half their program costs.
